covers.quote: Singular pronouns have a gender-neutral form.
‘they’ instead of ‘he’ or ‘she’
‘them’ instead of ‘him’ or ‘her’
‘their’ instead of ‘his’ or ‘hers’.

rules.specification: The listed replacements concern gender-neutral singular reference. The page does not specify when gender-neutral reference is required, so this should not become a blanket prohibition on gendered pronouns.
rules.violation_condition: A reference intended to be gender-neutral uses ‘he’ or ‘she’, ‘him’ or ‘her’, or ‘his’ or ‘hers’ instead of the corresponding listed gender-neutral form.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the subject, object and possessive replacements together as cases of one gender-neutral-reference rule.

rules.quote: When the singular ‘they’ is used in a sentence as a gender-neutral term, it takes the plural form of a verb.
rules.violation_condition: A verb agreeing with gender-neutral singular ‘they’ has a singular rather than a plural form.
when: When singular ‘they’ is used as a gender-neutral term and a verb agrees with it.
rules.why: The flag-and-cite test separates verb agreement from the neighbouring rules about pronoun forms.

covers.quote: The form of a pronoun will change depending on whether it is the subject or the object of the verb.
A pronoun used as the subject in a sentence is in the subjective case (for example, ‘I’, ‘they’).
A pronoun used as the object in a sentence is in the objective case (for example, ‘me’, ‘them’).

examples.note: Candidate heading excluded under G-4: it describes variation in pronoun forms; the actionable instructions are in the body.

rules.quote: Use the correct case when writing pronouns.
rules.violation_condition: An objective personal-pronoun form is used as a verb's subject, or a subjective personal-pronoun form is used as its object.
when: When choosing between the subjective and objective forms of a personal pronoun used as the subject or object of a verb.
rules.why: G-2 keeps subject and object cases together; G-4 selects the actionable body instruction rather than the descriptive heading.

covers.quote: Sentences can have reflexive pronouns when the subject is also the object of the verb.

examples.note: G-3 permission incorporated into the conditions of the reflexive-object prohibition.

rules.quote: Don’t use a reflexive pronoun if the subject and the object are not the same person or thing.
rules.violation_condition: A reflexive pronoun used as a verb's object refers to someone or something other than that verb's subject.
when: When a reflexive pronoun is used as the object of a verb.
A reflexive object is permitted when it refers to the same person or thing as the subject.
rules.why: G-3 records the same-referent permission as a condition of this prohibition, not as another rule.

examples.note: G-5 advice to inspect the sentence; the text requirement is captured by the preceding correct-case rule.

parts.quote: My colleague and I travelled with the delegation.

rules.quote: Don’t use reflexive pronouns such as ‘yourself’ and ‘myself’ as the subject of the verb.
rules.violation_condition: A reflexive pronoun is used as the subject of a verb, including as one member of a coordinated subject.
rules.why: The flag-and-cite test separates a reflexive pronoun's prohibited subject position from an object's failure to refer back to its subject.

covers.quote: ‘that’ for essential information
‘which’, with punctuation, for non-essential information.
Choosing between relative pronouns can be a matter of style in some situations, depending on voice and tone.

examples.note: G-3 stylistic flexibility qualifies the relative-pronoun preference; it is not an independently enforceable rule.

parts.quote: The farm that produces oats is for sale.

rules.quote: To make your writing clear, use:
rules.specification: Treat this as a preference when choosing between ‘that’ and ‘which’, not a prohibition on other relative pronouns such as ‘who’. The page leaves the voice-and-tone exceptions unspecified. Punctuation is a separate check.
rules.violation_condition: Essential relative information is introduced by ‘which’, or non-essential relative information by ‘that’, in a context where the stated stylistic preference applies.
when: When choosing between ‘that’ and ‘which’ as relative pronouns.
The choice may vary in some situations according to voice and tone.
rules.why: G-2 combines the essential and non-essential cases of relative-pronoun choice; G-3 preserves the stated stylistic flexibility.

covers.quote: ‘which’, with punctuation, for non-essential information.
It is the use of punctuation with the relative pronoun that clarifies meaning.

examples.note: G-4 punctuation guidance is absorbed into the separately stated punctuation rule; its pronoun-choice component supports the preference rule.

parts.quote: The farm that produces oats is for sale.

rules.quote: It is important to show users whether information is essential or non-essential by using punctuation, for example commas.
rules.violation_condition: Non-essential information introduced by a relative pronoun is not set off from the main clause by punctuation.
when: When a relative clause supplies non-essential information.
An essential relative clause does not require punctuation setting it off as non-essential.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the punctuation guidance; the flag-and-cite test separates missing punctuation from relative-pronoun choice.
